items.title: Effect of the vagus nerve stimulation combined with sound therapy for tinnitus treatment: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

evaluation.whatIsNew: First systematic review/meta-analysis to pool invasive and non-invasive VNS combined with sound therapy for tinnitus (8 studies reviewed, 6 pooled), reporting within-group pre-post improvements in THI (WMD 12.52) and VAS (WMD 11.21). The pooling itself is new; the underlying trials are largely already represented in the database and the analysis provides no between-group efficacy estimate.
evaluation.population: Patients with tinnitus enrolled in RCTs, observational studies and case studies of invasive or non-invasive (transcutaneous auricular) vagus nerve stimulation paired with sound/auditory stimulation; ages and tinnitus duration not specified in the abstract
evaluation.sampleSize: Not reported (8 studies in the systematic review, 6 in the meta-analysis; total participant N not given in the abstract)
evaluation.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) score; secondary pooled outcome was tinnitus VAS
evaluation.secondaryEndpoints: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) for tinnitus (scale anchor — loudness vs annoyance vs severity — not specified in the abstract)
evaluation.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — the pooled outcomes are THI (a handicap/distress questionnaire) and an unspecified VAS analysed within-group only; no psychoacoustic loudness matching is reported, and the VAS change did not even reach its own MCID, so nothing here supports an effect on the percept itself.
evaluation.distressEffect: limited — the pooled THI change exceeded the MCID, but it is an uncontrolled within-group pre-post pooling that cannot separate treatment effect from placebo, regression to the mean and natural fluctuation.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: A ~12.5-point THI drop would matter to patients if it were a true treatment effect, but in an uncontrolled within-group pooling of mixed designs (including case studies) that magnitude is well within what sham arms routinely produce in tinnitus trials, so no patient-relevant conclusion can be drawn.
evaluation.safetyObservations: Not reported — the abstract gives no adverse-event data for invasive or transcutaneous VNS
mainLimitations: Analysis based on within-group pre-post change, not between-group comparison — cannot estimate efficacy
Includes observational studies and case studies alongside RCTs; non-randomized evidence dominates
Pools fundamentally different interventions (surgically implanted paired VNS and transcutaneous auricular VNS) with different sound-pairing protocols
Total sample size, heterogeneity statistics, follow-up duration and publication-bias assessment not stated in the abstract
VAS anchor (loudness vs annoyance vs severity) unspecified; VAS improvement fell below MCID
No safety/adverse-event synthesis despite inclusion of an invasive surgical intervention
Authors themselves label the findings exploratory and not conclusive of comparative efficacy
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: independent — all authors are academic (Guilan University of Medical Sciences and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, Iran); competing interests declared as none; no device-manufacturer involvement stated, funding source not reported
evaluation.weeklyTitle: Review pools vagus nerve stimulation with sound therapy for tinnitus, but only measures uncontrolled before-and-after change
evaluation.whyMatters: This review adds up results from eight mostly small and uncontrolled studies of vagus nerve stimulation paired with sound, and finds that distress questionnaire scores improved after treatment. Because it compares people only to themselves rather than to a sham group, it cannot show that the device caused the improvement, and it says nothing about how loud the tinnitus actually was.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: Peer-reviewed primary record available (Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol, DOI 10.1007/s00405-026-10713-y, PMID 42867641) with methods, pooled effect estimates and COI statement given in the abstract; it is not a press release. Full text would be needed to verify included-study list, total N and heterogeneity.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: An independent Iranian meta-analysis pooling 6 studies of invasive and transcutaneous VNS plus sound therapy reports a within-group THI improvement of 12.5 points (above MCID) and a VAS improvement of 11.2 points (below MCID). The analysis is explicitly within-group only, mixes RCTs with observational and case reports, and lumps implanted paired VNS with taVNS — so it provides no comparative efficacy evidence and should not move vns-paired (score 2) or tavns (score 2). Recommend publishing as a labeled low-quality synthesis with the within-group caveat prominent; no loudness claim is supportable.

items.primaryRecordGivenToModel:
1. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2026 Oct 13. doi: 10.1007/s00405-026-10713-y.
Online  ahead of print.

Effect of the vagus nerve stimulation combined with sound therapy for tinnitus 
treatment: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Rezapour M(1), Jalali MM(2), Nemati S(1), Borna A(3).

Author information:
(1)Otorhinolaryngology Research Center, Department of Otolaryngology and Head 
and Neck Surgery, School of Medicine, Amiralmomenin Hospital, Guilan University 
of Medical Sciences, Rasht, Iran.
(2)Otorhinolaryngology Research Center, Department of Otolaryngology and Head 
and Neck Surgery, School of Medicine, Amiralmomenin Hospital, Guilan University 
of Medical Sciences, Rasht, Iran. mmjalali@gmail.com.
(3)Department of Audiology, School of Rehabilitation, Shahid Beheshti University 
of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran.

BACKGROUND: Tinnitus is a prevalent hearing problem linked to anxiety and 
depression. It currently has no cure. This systematic review and meta-analysis 
aimed to explore the potential association of combining vagus nerve stimulation 
(VNS) with auditory stimulation in alleviating tinnitus, recognizing the 
exploratory nature of evidence.
METHODS: Six databases were searched from 1990 to 2023 (2025 updated) for 
randomized clinical trials, observational studies, and case studies with at 
least one group receiving invasive or non-invasive VNS with sound for tinnitus 
management. Eligible studies used validated questionnaires to quantify tinnitus 
distress or severity in patients compared with controls or pre-treatment status. 
Two reviewers extracted participant, intervention, blinding, assessment, and 
outcome data. The risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for non-randomized 
studies and ROB2 for randomized controlled trials. PRISMA guidelines were 
followed.
RESULTS: Eight studies were included in the systematic review and six in the 
meta-analysis. The Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) and the Visual Analogue 
Scale (VAS) were suitable for meta-analysis. The analysis was primarily based on 
within-group pre‑post changes, not between‑group comparisons. For THI, the 
standardized mean difference (SMD) was 0.53 (95% CI: 0.12-0.94, p = 0.01), while 
the weighted mean difference (WMD) was 12.52 (95% CI: 4.56-20.48, p < 0.001), 
surpassing 7 minimal clinically important difference (MCID) threshold. For VAS, 
SMD was 0.55 (95% CI: 0.14-0.96, p = 0.01), but WMD was 11.21 (95% CI: 
4.79-17.63, p < 0.001) and the improvement fell short of the 15 MCID.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the limitations of an exploratory within‑group 
meta‑analysis, statistically and clinically significant reductions in THI were 
observed when VNS plus sound therapy. However, improvement in VAS was not 
clinically significant. These exploratory findings suggest a possible 
synergistic effect, but should not be considered conclusive evidence of 
comparative efficacy. Further controlled studies are needed.

items.title: Tinnitus outcomes after cochlear implantation in single-sided deafness: an exploratory prospective multicenter study.

evaluation.whatIsNew: A small Korean three-center prospective series (N=10) in which patients with single-sided deafness were implanted specifically to treat tinnitus, adding device-on versus device-off assessments and tinnitogram pitch/loudness matching; it reports that about half the patients showed a change in the psychoacoustic character of their tinnitus (pitch shift, or white noise becoming a tonal percept) after implantation. Otherwise it reproduces the already well-documented post-CI improvement in THI and tinnitus VAS.
evaluation.population: Adults with single-sided deafness and bothersome tinnitus who consented to cochlear implantation as a tinnitus treatment, recruited at three tertiary referral hospitals in Korea (Nov 2018–Jul 2020)
evaluation.primaryEndpoint: Not formally designated (explicitly exploratory); THI and tinnitus VAS at 3 months post-implantation, in device-on and device-off conditions
evaluation.secondaryEndpoints: Aided pure-tone audiometry and word recognition score; tinnitogram pitch and loudness matching; T-level/C-level at the pitch-matched frequency
evaluation.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
evaluation.numericalResult: THI: preoperative 78 → device-on 38 (p = 0.027), device-off 50 (p = 0.049). VAS: preoperative 8.2 → device-on 3.3 (p = 0.011), device-off 6.5 (p = 0.012). 4/10 patients showed changed psychoacoustic tinnitus features (2 lower frequency, 1 higher frequency, 1 white noise → identifiable tone). No significant tendency in T-level/C-level changes at the pitch-matched frequency.
evaluation.loudnessEffect: limited — a subjective VAS that includes a loudness item fell from 8.2 to 3.3 with the device on, but this is an uncontrolled, unblinded within-group change in 10 patients and the paper reports no quantitative pre/post psychoacoustic loudness-matching values, so it adds little beyond the existing 'moderate' loudness rating for cochlear implants.
evaluation.distressEffect: moderate — THI dropped from 78 (catastrophic) to 38 device-on and 50 device-off, consistent with the larger CI literature, but uncontrolled and in only 10 patients, so it confirms rather than extends the existing moderate distress rating.
evaluation.otherOutcomes: Aided PTA and word recognition score were measured post-CI but no values are given in the abstract; no sleep or quality-of-life instruments reported.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: A ~40-point THI drop and residual benefit with the device switched off would be clinically meaningful if real, but with N=10, no control group, no blinding and no accounting for regression to the mean or expectancy in patients who chose surgery for tinnitus, the effect size cannot be taken as an unbiased estimate.
evaluation.safetyObservations: Not reported — no surgical complications, adverse events or loss of residual hearing data are described in the record.
mainLimitations: Very small sample (N=10; 9 for device-off)
No non-implanted or alternative-device control group
No randomization and no blinding; patients self-selected surgery to treat tinnitus (strong expectancy bias)
Short follow-up (3 months)
Authors explicitly label findings exploratory and hypothesis-generating
Abstract does not report quantitative pre/post loudness-matching values, so 'loudness' rests on subjective VAS
VAS composite reporting makes it unclear which subscale (loudness, distress, perception) drove the change
Safety and audiologic outcome numbers not reported in the record reviewed
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: independent — authors declare no commercial or financial relationships; no manufacturer funding disclosed. A reviewer declared a past co-authorship with the senior author (editorial, minor).
evaluation.weeklyTitle: Small uncontrolled Korean study reports tinnitus improvement after cochlear implantation for single-sided deafness
evaluation.whyMatters: In 10 people with deafness in one ear who had a cochlear implant specifically to treat their tinnitus, tinnitus handicap scores and self-rated tinnitus fell markedly, with some benefit persisting even when the device was switched off. Because there was no comparison group and only 10 patients, this adds confirmation rather than new proof, and the authors themselves call it exploratory.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: Peer-reviewed primary article with DOI, PMID and PMC record; numbers quoted are taken directly from the published abstract. It can be reported as published, with the uncontrolled N=10 design stated.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: Small (N=10), uncontrolled, unblinded prospective multicenter cohort of cochlear implantation performed explicitly for tinnitus in single-sided deafness; THI 78→38 device-on / 50 device-off and VAS 8.2→3.3 / 6.5 at 3 months, plus an interesting observation that 4/10 patients' tinnitus pitch or character changed post-implant. This is consistent with the existing ci-meta-2024 and CINGLE evidence and does not justify any change to the cochlear-implant score (3), tier (2) or loudness/distress ratings — the loudness signal here is a subjective VAS, not reported psychoacoustic matching. Recommend publishing as a 'confirms previous evidence' item with the small-sample, no-control caveat stated up front.

items.primaryRecordGivenToModel:
1. Front Neurol. 2026 Sep 28;17:1970581. doi: 10.3389/fneur.2026.1970581. 
eCollection 2026.

Tinnitus outcomes after cochlear implantation in single-sided deafness: an 
exploratory prospective multicenter study.

Song JJ(1), Choi Y(2), Kim Y(2), Lee JH(1), Park HJ(2), Chung JW(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Seoul National 
University Hospital, Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul, 
Republic of Korea.
(2)Department of Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Asan Medical Center, 
University of Ulsan College of Medicine, Seoul, Republic of Korea.

Tinnitus is thought to be suppressed through partial reversal of auditory 
deafferentation via cochlear implantation (CI). By stimulating the deafferented 
auditory pathway, multiple studies have revealed that tinnitus is significantly 
suppressed in 66-92% of patients undergoing CI. This study aimed to evaluate the 
efficacy of CI as a treatment for tinnitus and to investigate post-CI audiologic 
outcomes in patients with single-sided deafness (SSD). From November 2018 to 
July 2020, 10 patients who were diagnosed with SSD and suffering from tinnitus 
were prospectively recruited at three tertiary referral hospitals. Participants 
in this study agreed to undergo CI as a treatment for tinnitus. Postoperative 
aided pure tone audiometry (PTA) and word recognition score (WRS) were measured. 
Questionnaires related to tinnitus, such as the tinnitus handicap inventory 
(THI) and visual analogue scale (VAS) scores including loudness, distress, and 
perception, were administered. Additionally, a tinnitogram was obtained for 
loudness and pitch matching. Audiological outcomes of CI were analyzed in 
conjunction with the results of pitch-matching from the tinnitogram. All 10 
patients completed device-on evaluations, and 9 patients completed device-off 
evaluations. THI scores showed statistically significant improvement 3 months 
after CI in both the device-on and device-off conditions (preoperative: 78; 
device on: 38, p = 0.027; device off: 50, p = 0.049). VAS scores also 
demonstrated significant improvement after CI (preoperative: 8.2; device on: 
3.3, p = 0.011; device off: 6.5, p = 0.012). Four patients demonstrated changes 
in psychoacoustic tinnitus features after CI: 2 changed to lower frequency, 1 
changed to higher frequency, and 1 patient's tinnitus changed from white noise 
to a specific identifiable frequency. There was no significant tendency for 
threshold (T-level and C-level) changes in pitch-matching frequency. In line 
with previous literature, this exploratory multicenter study demonstrated 
improvement in tinnitus loudness and distress after CI in patients with 
single-sided deafness and tinnitus, with a tendency for greater reduction in 
tinnitus intensity observed when the device was activated. Additionally, 
approximately half of the patients showed changes in the psychoacoustic 
characteristics of tinnitus after CI. Given the small sample size and the 
absence of a non-implanted control group, these findings should be regarded as 
exploratory and hypothesis-generating, and warrant confirmation in adequately 
powered controlled trials.

Copyright © 2026 Song, Choi, Kim, Lee, Park and Chung.

items.title: Acute Nicotine Gum and Auditory Brain Responses in Adults With Chronic Tinnitus

evaluation.whatIsNew: A newly posted ClinicalTrials.gov registration (not yet recruiting) for a small investigator-initiated, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study testing whether a single 4 mg dose of nicotine gum alters auditory oddball P3, task performance and resting-state EEG in 20 non-smoking adults with chronic tinnitus. No results exist; the registry notes it is a separate study under the same IRB protocol as the completed NCT07772089, which looked at acute nicotine gum effects on tinnitus loudness and attention.
evaluation.population: Non-smoking adults aged 18-80 with chronic subjective tinnitus (≥6 months), Fagerström ≤2 and negative urinary cotinine; excludes current nicotine users, pregnancy, unstable cardiovascular disease
evaluation.primaryEndpoint: Auditory oddball P3 amplitude and latency, plus oddball target-detection accuracy and reaction time, measured after gum administration (nicotine vs placebo)
evaluation.secondaryEndpoints: Resting-state EEG spectral power (delta–gamma) and aperiodic 1/f slope; oddball sensitivity (d'). Exploratory/other: within-session change in psychoacoustic tinnitus loudness match (dB SL), baseline THI, TFI and pure-tone audiometry
evaluation.comparisonType: Not reported — no results posted; the planned analysis is a within-subject crossover comparison of nicotine vs placebo sessions
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — tinnitus loudness matching is only an exploratory 'other' outcome in a trial that has not yet begun enrolling, so this registration says nothing about whether nicotine changes the loudness of the percept.
evaluation.distressEffect: none — THI and TFI are collected once at baseline for characterisation only and are not outcome measures of change.
evaluation.otherOutcomes: Baseline pure-tone audiometry (0.25–12 kHz) for characterisation only; no sleep, QoL or hearing-change outcomes planned.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: No clinical significance can be assigned: this is a single-dose mechanistic EEG/attention study with no therapeutic endpoint, no durability assessment, and no results.
evaluation.safetyObservations: Not reported — no data exist; the protocol excludes unstable cardiovascular disease, pregnancy and breastfeeding, and lists no data monitoring committee (oversightHasDmc: false) for a single 4 mg over-the-counter nicotine dose.
mainLimitations: Registration only — not yet recruiting, no participants, no results
Very small planned sample (n=20) for a crossover with multiple EEG and behavioural primary endpoints
Primary purpose is explicitly BASIC_SCIENCE: endpoints are P3/EEG and attention, not tinnitus relief
Four co-primary outcomes across four electrodes with no stated multiplicity correction or power calculation in the record
Single acute dose with outcomes measured within ~2 hours; no information on durability or repeated dosing
Tinnitus loudness relegated to exploratory 'other' outcome; THI/TFI measured at baseline only
Blinding of an acute nicotine dose in nicotine-naive adults may be imperfect despite flavour-matched placebo, given stimulant and nausea effects
Single site, single sponsor-investigator, no independent replication
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: independent — sponsor-investigator Xianhui Wang (San Diego State University), no listed industry sponsor or collaborator; commercial products (Nicorette, Trident) are used as intervention and placebo but no manufacturer funding is declared in the record.
evaluation.weeklyTitle: Registered: small placebo-controlled study of a single dose of nicotine gum and brain responses to sound in people with tinnitus
evaluation.whyMatters: Researchers have registered a small, properly blinded crossover experiment to see whether one piece of nicotine gum changes how the brain responds to sounds in people with chronic tinnitus. It is a mechanism study, not a treatment trial — it has not started, has no results, and is not a reason to try nicotine for tinnitus.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: The item is an authoritative ClinicalTrials.gov primary record (NCT07877701, first posted 2026-10-16) and can be reported factually as a registration; the reported facts are limited to design, status and planned endpoints, with no efficacy claims to verify.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: Registry-only entry for a not-yet-recruiting, investigator-initiated n=20 double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study of a single 4 mg nicotine gum dose in non-smoking adults with chronic tinnitus; primary endpoints are auditory oddball P3 and task performance, i.e. mechanism/measurement rather than treatment efficacy. Tinnitus loudness matching is an exploratory outcome and THI/TFI are baseline descriptors only, so nothing here touches any loudness or distress rating. File as tinnitus-specific science and as a watch-item candidate (nicotinic/cholinergic modulation); no score or tier change, and note the companion completed trial NCT07772089 is not yet in the database and should be tracked.

items.title: Fluid Management of Acute Decompensated Heart Failure Subjects Treated With Reprieve System (FASTR-II) (IDE-G210258)

evaluation.whatIsNew: Nothing of tinnitus relevance: this is a routine ClinicalTrials.gov status update (still RECRUITING) for FASTR-II, a cardiology device trial of the Reprieve System for fluid management in acute decompensated heart failure. Tinnitus appears only as one of several safety/tolerability secondary endpoints tracking loop-diuretic ototoxicity.
evaluation.population: Adults ≥22 years hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure, ≥10 lb above dry weight, on outpatient loop diuretics, with markers of elevated diuretic-resistance risk
evaluation.primaryEndpoint: Hierarchical composite/win-ratio (freedom from 30-day CV mortality; freedom from HF rehospitalization within 30 days of discharge; greater net sodium loss per 24 hours), plus incidence of device/procedure-related adverse events (KDIGO stage ≥2 AKI, CAUTI)
evaluation.secondaryEndpoints: Net sodium loss, time to discharge readiness, time on IV diuretics, net fluid loss, weight loss, CV mortality/HF rehospitalizations at 90 days, length of stay, hypotension, severe electrolyte abnormality, worsening heart failure, and 'tinnitus or hearing loss lasting more than 30 minutes' (a diuretic ototoxicity safety measure)
evaluation.comparisonType: Not reported — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
evaluation.numericalResult: none reported (trial recruiting; primary completion estimated August 2027, no results posted)
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — no tinnitus loudness measurement of any kind; tinnitus is captured only as a binary adverse-event occurrence (>30 minutes) related to furosemide ototoxicity.
evaluation.distressEffect: none — no THI/TFI or any tinnitus distress instrument is used.
evaluation.otherOutcomes: Cardiovascular and renal outcomes only (decongestion efficiency, mortality, rehospitalization, AKI, electrolytes); no hearing or audiometric outcomes beyond the binary tinnitus/hearing-loss adverse-event item.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: No results exist yet, and even on completion the design cannot inform any tinnitus treatment decision — at most it may eventually add a small datapoint on loop-diuretic ototoxicity rates under automated versus guideline-titrated furosemide dosing.
evaluation.safetyObservations: Not reported — no safety data posted; the trial is recruiting with a DMC in place and prespecifies AKI, CAUTI, hypotension, electrolyte abnormality and transient tinnitus/hearing loss as monitored events.
mainLimitations: Not a tinnitus study — tinnitus is an incidental ototoxicity safety checkbox in a heart-failure device trial
No results posted; recruiting, primary completion estimated August 2027
Tinnitus captured only as a binary >30-minute adverse event, with no loudness matching, no validated questionnaire, and no audiometry
Only outcomes-assessor blinding; patients and treating clinicians unblinded
Industry-sponsored device trial of an unapproved device
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: manufacturer-funded / author equity — lead sponsor and responsible party is Reprieve Cardiovascular, Inc, the device manufacturer; investigator COI not available from the registry record. Irrelevant to tinnitus evidence here, but noted.
evaluation.weeklyTitle: Heart-failure fluid-management device trial lists tinnitus only as a diuretic side-effect check (no tinnitus findings)
evaluation.whyMatters: This is a cardiology trial of an automated diuretic-infusion device; it tracks tinnitus only as a known short-term side effect of high-dose furosemide. It tells us nothing about treating tinnitus and should not appear as tinnitus evidence.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: The ClinicalTrials.gov primary record (NCT06898515) is authoritative and confirms the status change to RECRUITING and the trial design; however, the item is tinnitus-incidental (category 5) and therefore should not reach the public feed regardless of verification.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: False positive from the news-wire keyword sweep: FASTR-II is a 400-patient randomized heart-failure decongestion device trial (Reprieve Cardiovascular), and 'tinnitus' appears solely as a secondary safety endpoint for loop-diuretic ototoxicity. The update is purely administrative (status RECRUITING, last update 13 Oct 2026); no results, no tinnitus data. Recommend filing as not relevant with no changes to any treatment score, tier, or loudness/distress rating.

items.title: Cilcare Opens Tokyo Subsidiary to Drive Asia-Pacific Hearing Health Expansion - The Hearing Review

evaluation.whatIsNew: Cilcare, a hearing-health biotech with a tinnitus program (CIL001) already logged as a company-reported development, announced the opening of a Tokyo subsidiary for Asia-Pacific business expansion. This is corporate/commercial news with no clinical data, no trial results, and no regulatory filing attached.
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic or perceptual measurement of any kind is involved in a corporate expansion announcement.
evaluation.distressEffect: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or any patient-reported outcome is involved.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: No clinical significance whatsoever; opening a regional office tells patients nothing about whether any Cilcare compound works.
mainLimitations: Not a study — corporate business announcement
No primary record available; evaluated from news-wire metadata only
No clinical, mechanistic or regulatory content
Secondary trade-press reporting of a company statement
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: manufacturer-funded / company self-reported — the item originates from Cilcare itself via trade press (The Hearing Review); inherently promotional.
evaluation.weeklyTitle: Cilcare opens Tokyo subsidiary (company-reported business expansion)
evaluation.whyMatters: A hearing-health company that is working on an early tinnitus drug candidate has opened an office in Japan. This is a business move, not a scientific result, and says nothing about whether their treatment helps tinnitus.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: Only a Google News RSS headline and company-sourced trade-press summary were available; no primary record, company press release page, or registry entry was fetched to confirm the announcement's details. The underlying fact (a corporate subsidiary opening) is plausible and low-stakes but remains unverified from a primary source.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: Pure corporate expansion news from Cilcare (Tokyo subsidiary) — intelligenceOnly in spirit and in practice: no data, no endpoints, no regulatory record. It cannot strengthen cilcare-cil001 or any rating and should not enter the evidence feed; at most it is a labeled company-reported development once the announcement itself is confirmed from a primary source. Recommend no change to any treatment, tier, or score.

items.primaryRecordGivenToModel: (no primary record fetcher for this source; evaluate from the metadata alone and lower confidence)

items.title: Efficacy of acupuncture for tinnitus with anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

evaluation.whatIsNew: A new meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 908 patients, mostly Chinese-language) pooling acupuncture trials specifically in patients with tinnitus plus comorbid anxiety, adding anxiety scales (HAMA/SAS/BAI) and serum biomarkers (BDNF, 5-HT, GABA) to the familiar tinnitus-questionnaire outcomes. The biomarker analyses were all null, and the clinical outcomes rest on the same low-quality 'total effective rate' / TCM-syndrome-score literature already reflected in the database.
evaluation.population: Adults with subjective tinnitus accompanied by anxiety, enrolled in randomized trials predominantly conducted in China
evaluation.primaryEndpoint: Total effective rate for tinnitus with anxiety (composite responder rate; definition not standardized across trials)
evaluation.secondaryEndpoints: Tinnitus Severity Questionnaire (TEQ), THI, TCM syndrome scores, HAMA, SAS, BAI, and serum BDNF, 5-HT and GABA levels
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating of the percept was pooled; TEQ, THI and 'total effective rate' are severity/handicap constructs and cannot be read as loudness reduction.
evaluation.distressEffect: limited — pooled THI (−9.11) and anxiety-scale reductions favour acupuncture, but they come from small, unblinded, high-risk-of-bias trials in a literature with well-documented positive-result bias, so this does not establish a reliable distress benefit.
evaluation.otherOutcomes: Serum biomarkers (BDNF, 5-HT, GABA) showed no significant between-group differences, undercutting the proposed mechanism; sleep and quality-of-life outcomes Not reported.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: A pooled THI change of about 9 points sits only marginally above the usual ~7-point minimal detectable change and is derived from unblinded trials with a non-standardized 'total effective rate' outcome, so patient-meaningful benefit remains unproven.
evaluation.safetyObservations: Not reported — the abstract provides no adverse-event data from the included trials.
mainLimitations: Included trials are small, predominantly Chinese-language, and almost certainly unblinded with no sham-acupuncture control
'Total effective rate' and TCM syndrome scores are non-standardized, non-validated composite outcomes
Known strong positive-result/publication bias in the regional acupuncture literature; no publication-bias assessment reported in the abstract
No psychoacoustic loudness outcome at all
No follow-up duration reported; durability unknown
Null biomarker results contradict the mechanistic rationale offered
Heterogeneity in acupuncture protocols, comparators and anxiety instruments not quantified in the abstract
No independent replication outside the same research tradition
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: independent — authors declare no commercial or financial relationships; however all authors are from acupuncture departments of TCM-affiliated hospitals, an orientation bias worth noting. PROSPERO-registered (CRD42024596594).
evaluation.weeklyTitle: New meta-analysis of acupuncture for tinnitus with anxiety reports benefits, but from low-quality unblinded trials
evaluation.whyMatters: This review pools 12 mostly small Chinese trials and reports that acupuncture improved tinnitus questionnaire and anxiety scores, but none of the trials appear to have used sham acupuncture or blinding, and the blood markers the authors expected to change did not. It does not show any effect on how loud the tinnitus sound itself is, and it is not strong enough to move acupuncture up our evidence ranking.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: Peer-reviewed primary record indexed in MEDLINE with DOI, PMCID and a PROSPERO registration; the numbers reported here are taken directly from the published abstract, so the factual report can be published even though it changes nothing.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: Another acupuncture meta-analysis, this time scoped to tinnitus with comorbid anxiety (12 RCTs, N=908). It reports positive pooled effects on total effective rate, TEQ, THI and anxiety scales but null results on BDNF, 5-HT and GABA; the underlying trials are small, unblinded, sham-free and dominated by Chinese-language sources using non-validated 'total effective rate' and TCM syndrome outcomes. Consistent with the existing acupuncture umbrella review in the database — keep acupuncture at tier 5, score 2, loudness 'none', distress 'none'; publish as a routine feed item only.

items.primaryRecordGivenToModel:
1. Front Neurol. 2026 Sep 22;17:1920000. doi: 10.3389/fneur.2026.1920000. 
eCollection 2026.

Efficacy of acupuncture for tinnitus with anxiety: a systematic review and 
meta-analysis.

Peiyun W(#)(1), Shuaihui Q(#)(2), Yi C(3), Hao Y(3).

Author information:
(1)Acupuncture Department, Wuxi Second People's Hospital, Wuxi, Jiangsu, China.
(2)Acupuncture Department, Wuxi Second Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, 
Wuxi, Jiangsu, China.
(3)Acupuncture Department, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Anhui University of 
Chinese Medicine, Hefei, Anhui, China.
(#)Contributed equally

BACKGROUND: Evidence suggests that acupuncture can alleviate tinnitus symptoms 
and improve the anxiety associated with tinnitus, but the relationship between 
these outcomes is unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy of acupuncture for tinnitus with anxiety 
using a meta-analysis.
METHODS: Computerized searches were conducted in nine databases: China National 
Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, VIP Chinese Science and 
Technology Journal Full-text Database, SinoMed, Chinese Medical Journal 
Full-text Database (CMAJD), PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of 
Science. The search covered the period from the establishment of each database 
to January 15, 2026. Relevant randomized controlled trials meeting the inclusion 
and exclusion criteria were selected. The Cochrane Collaboration's recommended 
methods were used to assess the quality of included studies. Outcomes evaluated 
included the total effective rate, Tinnitus Severity Questionnaire (TEQ), 
Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI), Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome scores 
(TCM syndrome scores), Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale 
(SAS), Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), 
serum 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), and serum gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) 
levels as outcome measures. Meta-analysis was performed using ReMan 5.3 
software.
RESULTS: Twelve studies involving 908 patients were included. Meta-analysis 
revealed that acupuncture demonstrated superiority in improving the total 
effective rate for tinnitus with anxiety (RR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.10-1.26, P < 
0.00001) and significantly reduced TEQ scores (MD = -1.96, 95% CI: -2.47 to 
-1.45, Z = 7.57, P < 0.00001), and THI (MD = -9.11, 95% CI: -12.89 to -5.34, Z = 
4.73, P < 0.00001), TCM syndrome scores (MD = -0.59, 95% CI: -1.13 to -0.06, Z = 
2.17, P = 0.03 < 0.05), HAMA (MD = -2.04, 95% CI: -3.08 to -1.00, Z = 3.84, P = 
0.0001 < 0.05) scores, SAS (MD = -3.50, 95% CI: -6.22 to -0.77, Z = 2.52, P = 
0.01 < 0.05), BAI (MD = -8.80, 95% CI: -13.48 to -4.12, Z = 3.68, P = 0.0002 < 
0.05) scores, but not in improving BDNF (MD = -72.27, 95% CI: -312.41 to 167.87, 
Z = 0.59, P = 0.56 > 0.05), 5-HT (MD = -22.56, 95% CI: -56.12 to 10.99, Z = 
1.32, P = 0.19 > 0.05), and GABA (MD = 56.23, 95% CI: -46.50 to 158.96, Z = 
1.07, P = 0.28 > 0.05) levels.
CONCLUSIONS: Acupuncture treatment for tinnitus with anxiety demonstrated 
greater improvement than non-acupuncture approaches in enhancing the clinical 
total effective rate and reducing TEQ, THI, TCM syndrome scores, BAI, HAMA, and 
SAS scores, warranting clinical promotion. However, evidence levels for certain 
outcome measures (BDNF, 5-HT, and GABA) remain low, necessitating further 
validation through well-designed, methodologically rigorous, high-quality, 
large-scale randomized controlled trials.

items.title: Correction: Objective measurement of tinnitus using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and machine learning.

evaluation.whatIsNew: Nothing new clinically — this is a published correction (erratum) to a 2020 PLoS One paper on fNIRS plus machine learning as an objective tinnitus measure; the correction notice itself contains no new data, methods or results.
evaluation.population: Not reported (original 2020 study examined adults with and without tinnitus; correction notice gives no population detail)
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — a correction notice to a diagnostic/measurement paper provides no data on the loudness of the tinnitus percept.
evaluation.distressEffect: none — no distress instrument (THI/TFI/TQ) data is reported in this item.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: No clinical effect of any kind is reported; even the underlying 2020 work is an exploratory measurement/classification study, not a treatment.
mainLimitations: Erratum/correction notice only — no new data, no abstract, no results
Underlying 2020 paper is a small exploratory diagnostic/biomarker study, not treatment evidence
Nature and materiality of the correction cannot be judged from this record alone; the corrected article should be re-read before citing
No independent replication of fNIRS+ML tinnitus classification established
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: unclear — correction notice does not restate funding or COI; authors are affiliated with the Bionics Institute (hearing-device research environment), so the original article's COI/funding statement should be checked directly.
evaluation.weeklyTitle: Correction issued to 2020 study on fNIRS plus machine learning as an objective tinnitus measure
evaluation.whyMatters: Researchers have published a formal correction to an older paper that tested whether brain-imaging signals plus machine learning could objectively detect tinnitus. It is a housekeeping notice, not a new finding, and it does not affect any treatment recommendation.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: The PubMed/PLoS One record is a primary, citable source (PMID 42821511, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0359852) confirming an erratum for DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0241695; the existence and nature of the correction are verifiable, even though the correction's substance is not summarized in the record.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: This is a correction notice to Shoushtarian et al. 2020, an exploratory fNIRS + machine-learning study aimed at objectively measuring tinnitus — measurement science, not treatment evidence (category 2). It contains no new data, population, or outcomes, and affects no treatment entry, score, tier, or loudness/distress rating. File as context only; if the fNIRS biomarker line is ever added as a measurement topic, pull and read the corrected 2020 article (including its funding/COI statement) rather than relying on this notice.

items.title: The CATT Trial: Cost-effectiveness of a Smartphone Application for Tinnitus Treatment

evaluation.whatIsNew: The CATT trial (NCT05245318) registry record now shows COMPLETED status with 241 actual participants enrolled (primary completion May 2025, study completion November 2025); no results are posted yet. Genuinely new is only the status/enrollment/date change — a sizeable somatic-tinnitus physiotherapy trial has finished and a readout should follow.
evaluation.population: Adults diagnosed with somatic (somatosensory) tinnitus, without psychiatric comorbidity, recruited at the ENT department of Antwerp University Hospital (Belgium)
evaluation.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI) from baseline to one month after the last treatment session (a DISTRESS/impact measure, not loudness)
evaluation.secondaryEndpoints: VAS tinnitus loudness, psychoacoustic tinnitus pitch and loudness matching, Neck Bournemouth Questionnaire, TMD pain screener, clinical neck/jaw tests, cervical range of motion (NeckCare), pure-tone audiometry, speech-in-quiet/speech-in-noise, HADS, Hyperacusis Questionnaire, plus cost-effectiveness (EQ-5D, iMTA PCQ)
evaluation.numericalResult: none reported — no outcome data posted on the registry; only status (COMPLETED) and actual enrollment (241) are available
evaluation.loudnessEffect: none — no outcome data exist yet; the trial does include VAS loudness and psychoacoustic loudness matching as secondary measures, so a future publication could inform the loudness column, but nothing can be concluded now.
evaluation.distressEffect: none — the TFI primary endpoint is a distress/impact measure, but no results have been reported.
evaluation.otherOutcomes: Planned but unreported: hearing/speech measures, neck and jaw pain and mobility, anxiety/depression (HADS), hyperacusis, quality of life (EQ-5D) and a formal cost-effectiveness analysis including productivity costs.
evaluation.clinicalSignificance: Cannot be assessed — no effect sizes are available; note also the non-inferiority design means a 'positive' result would show that app-supported delivery with half the clinic visits matches standard physiotherapy, not that physiotherapy itself beats no treatment.
evaluation.safetyObservations: Not reported — the registry record notes an independent data monitoring committee (oversightHasDmc: true) but posts no adverse-event data.
mainLimitations: No results posted; status change only
Non-inferiority design against an active physiotherapy comparator, so it cannot establish efficacy of physiotherapy per se for somatic tinnitus
Therapist cannot be blinded (visit frequency differs); blinding limited to participants' allocation awareness and a blinded assessor — patient blinding is in practice questionable
Single-centre recruitment (Antwerp University Hospital), selected population excluding psychiatric comorbidity and smartphone-naive patients
Primary endpoint is distress (TFI) at 1 month post-treatment with only 3-month follow-up — short durability window
Mixes two interventions (app-delivered exercise + tinnitus counselling) so components cannot be disentangled
evaluation.conflictOfInterest: independent — academic sponsor (Hasselt University; PI Prof. Sarah Michiels) with university/hospital collaborators (Antwerp, UZA, Regensburg); no manufacturer sponsor listed on the registry record. App developer/commercial involvement not disclosed in the record and should be checked at publication.
evaluation.weeklyTitle: CATT trial of app-supported physiotherapy for somatic tinnitus completes with 241 participants; results not yet posted
evaluation.whyMatters: A reasonably large randomised trial testing whether a smartphone app plus half as many physiotherapy visits works as well as standard weekly physiotherapy for neck/jaw-related tinnitus has finished recruiting and treating patients. Nothing can be concluded until the results are published — this is a note that a readout is coming.
evaluation.factuallyVerifiedReason: The ClinicalTrials.gov record itself is an authoritative primary source for the facts being reported (status COMPLETED, 241 actual enrolled, completion dates, design and outcome measures). Those facts are verified; no efficacy claim is being made because none is available.
evaluation.summaryForAdmin: Registry status update only: the academic CATT non-inferiority RCT (app-blended vs standard physiotherapy for somatic tinnitus, n=241, TFI primary) is now marked COMPLETED with no results posted. No score, tier, loudness or distress change is warranted — file as a pending-readout watch item under somatic-physio (with secondary relevance to digital-cbt-style delivery). Worth re-reviewing when the publication appears, especially since psychoacoustic loudness matching is among the secondary outcomes.
